desc:
You are given a sequence seq of integers and a list patterns of distinct non-empty integer sequences (each row of patterns is one pattern). A cutting splits seq into consecutive non-empty pieces so that every piece is exactly equal to one of the patterns. A pattern may be used any number of times.

Return the number of different cuttings, modulo 1,000,000,007. Two cuttings are different if they put cuts at different positions. Return 0 if no cutting exists.

seq = [1,2,1,2], patterns = [[1],[2],[1,2]]  -> 4   (1|2|1|2, 12|1|2, 1|2|12, 12|12)
seq = [1,1,1],   patterns = [[1],[1,1]]      -> 3   (1|1|1, 11|1, 1|11)
seq = [1,2],     patterns = [[2],[3]]        -> 0
constraints: 1 ≤ patterns.length ≤ 300; 1 ≤ patterns[i].length ≤ 10; all patterns are distinct
hints: This is the 'word break' question where you have to count instead of decide. Think about which piece comes last.
Let ways[i] be the number of cuttings of the first i numbers, with ways[0] = 1 for the empty prefix.

ways[i] is the sum of ways[i - L] over all pattern lengths L for which the last L numbers of the prefix equal a pattern. Store the patterns as tuples in a set so the comparison is one lookup, and only try the distinct lengths.
editorial: Count prefix cuttings. Let ways[0] = 1. For a prefix of length i, the last piece is a pattern that ends at position i; if it has length L and equals seq[i-L:i], the part before it can be cut in ways[i-L] ways. Adding these over all matching patterns gives ways[i]. Distinct patterns of equal length cannot both match the same slice, so nothing is counted twice.

Put each pattern (as a tuple) in a hash set and keep the sorted list of distinct lengths (at most 10). For each end position and each length, build the slice as a tuple and test membership. That is about n · 10 lookups of length at most 10, so the cost is O(n · D · L) where D is the number of distinct lengths and L the longest pattern. Remember to take everything modulo 1,000,000,007.
